module-7-quick-review-optional.title: Module 7 Quick Review (optional)
module-7-quick-review-optional.body:
Optional quick review, about a two-minute read. Not graded. For more detail, see the full Chapter Review page.

Formulas to know
  • Warranty liability: beginning + expense accrued − claims paid = ending
  • Interest = principal × annual rate × time
  • Bond price = PV of coupons (annuity) + PV of face value (lump sum), at the market rate per period
  • Interest expense (effective interest) = carrying value × market rate per period
  • Discount amortized = interest expense − cash coupon
  • Times interest earned = operating income ÷ interest expense
  • PV of a single amount = future value ÷ (1 + r)^n

1. Accrued liabilities and the warranty liability

  • An accrued liability is an obligation for an expense the company has incurred but not yet paid. The expense is recorded when it is incurred.
  • Warranty liability rollforward: beginning + expense accrued − claims paid = ending.
  • Warranty expense is usually estimated as a percent of net sales, then compared with actual claims. A growing liability means the company is accruing more than it pays out.

2. Contingent liabilities: accrue, disclose or ignore?

  • Probable and can be reasonably estimated: record the liability and the expense, and disclose it.
  • Reasonably possible (or probable but cannot be estimated): disclose in the footnotes, but do not record a liability.
  • Remote: no accrual and usually no disclosure.

3. Short-term borrowings, interest and the current portion of long-term debt

  • Interest = principal × annual rate × time. Use the average balance when the balance changed during the year.
  • A revolving credit line can be borrowed, repaid and borrowed again. Amounts due within a year are short-term.
  • The current portion of long-term debt is the principal due in the next 12 months. The rest stays long-term.

4. Coupon rate, market rate and bond prices

  • The coupon (stated) rate sets the cash interest. The market (yield) rate is what investors require, and it sets the price.
  • Coupon below market: the bond sells at a discount. Coupon above market: premium. Coupon equal to market: par.
  • Price = present value of the coupons (an annuity) + present value of the face value (a lump sum), both discounted at the market rate per period.

5. Interest expense on a discount bond (effective interest)

  • Interest expense = carrying value × market rate per period. The cash paid is face value × coupon rate per period.
  • Discount amortized = interest expense − cash coupon. It is added to the carrying value.
  • The carrying value rises toward the face value, so interest expense rises slightly each period.

6. Credit analysis: can Cullowhee handle more debt?

  • Times interest earned (TIE) = operating income ÷ interest expense. It shows how many times earnings cover interest.
  • Lenders also look at capital structure (debt to equity) and liquidity. Loan covenants often set a minimum TIE.
  • Credit ratings estimate the risk of default. A lower rating means a higher risk premium and a higher interest rate.

7. Time value of money

  • Present value of a single amount = future value ÷ (1 + r)n (or future value × a table factor).
  • An annuity is the same payment each period. Its present value = payment × annuity factor.
  • A higher rate or a longer wait lowers present value. The bond price on the previous cards used both a single-amount factor and an annuity factor.

Optional review. Not graded. The running example is Verizon (fiscal 2022, $ millions), as in the lectures and textbook.

What this module covers
LOLearning objective
7-1Evaluate accounting for accrued liabilities.
7-2Analyze short-term debt.
7-3Analyze long-term debt pricing.
7-4Analyze long-term debt.
7-5Explain how quality of debt is determined.
7-6Apply time value of money concepts.
Running example: Verizon Communications, fiscal 2022 (all dollar amounts in millions unless noted), with supporting examples from Harley-Davidson (warranty reserves) and the present-value tables in Appendix A.

The Big Picture: Liabilities by Certainty and by Maturity

Current (within a year)Long-term
Amount is known by contractWages payable, interest payable, taxes payable, deferred revenue, short-term notes, current maturities of long-term debt (LOs 7-1, 7-2)Bonds and notes payable, reported net of discount or including premium (LOs 7-3, 7-4)
Amount must be estimatedContingent liabilities — warranties, recalls, litigation — accrued when probable and reasonably estimable (LO 7-1)Accrued when the same two conditions are met

Two threads run through the module. First, an accrual is recognized in the period it is incurred, not the period it is paid — which is why the balance sheet carries liabilities that never came from an external transaction. Second, the price of debt is the present value of its cash flows (LOs 7-3 and 7-6), which is why the coupon rate a company prints on a bond does not determine what that debt actually costs.

What accrued liabilities are

Also called accrued expenses, or accruals.

  • Accrued liabilities are adjustments made to the balance sheet: after all transactions have been recorded, prior to the issuance of the financial statements, so that the statements fairly present the financial condition of the company.
  • These adjustments recognize liabilities (and the related expense on the income statement) that are not the result of external transactions.
  • Accrued liabilities are incurred in the current period and therefore must be recognized in the current period.

Two broad categories of accruals

CategoryExamples
Routine contractual liabilitiesWages to employees for work performed but not yet paid; unpaid interest due in the current period; income taxes owed but not yet paid on profit earned in the period; other expense items such as rent and utilities, incurred but not yet paid
Contingent liabilitiesDepend on the occurrence of a future uncertain event to determine whether a liability exists and in what amount: litigation brought against the company (outcome and amount depend on adjudication); warranty liabilities for products sold (the amount depends on future claims for repair or replacement)

Contractual accruals — wages payable

If the liability for unpaid wages is not reflected on the balance sheet:

  • Liabilities will be understated
  • Wage expense will not be reflected in the income statement
  • Profit for the period will be overstated

To correct for this, accountants make an accounting adjustment. When wages are later paid, cash and wages payable both decrease.

TransactionBalance sheet effectIncome statement effect
Period 1: Accrued $75 for employee wages earned at period-endLiabilities +75 (Wages Payable); Earned capital −75 (Retained Earnings)Expenses +75 (Wages Expense); Net income −75
Period 2: Paid $75 for wages earned in prior periodCash asset −75; Liabilities −75 (Wages Payable)None

Contractual accruals — deferred revenue

Also called unearned revenue.

  • Deferred revenue represents deposits or other prepayments from customers that the company has not yet earned.
  • Deferred revenue is an accrued liability until the company provides the goods or performs the service according to the contract.
  • Once the company satisfies the performance obligations, the liability is reduced and (earned) revenue is recognized.

Contingent liabilities

Some liabilities are less certain, because the ultimate settlement depends on the outcome of a future event. Examples include guarantees on the debt of another entity, lawsuits, product warranties and recalls, and environmental disasters and remediation.

A contingent liability is recorded when BOTH conditions are met:
1. It is probable that one or more future events will confirm that a liability existed at the financial statement date
2. The amount required to settle the liability in the future can be reasonably determined at the financial statement date

Warranties

  • Warranty liabilities are commitments manufacturers make to repair or replace defective products within a specified period of time.
  • If the obligation is probable and the amount estimable with reasonable certainty, GAAP requires companies to record the expected cost of warranties as a liability, and to record the related warranty expense in the same period that the sales revenue is reported.
  • When the defective product is later replaced or repaired, the liability is reduced and the company records the cost necessary to satisfy the claim.

Worked example. Sales during the period are $10,000; 2% of sales are defective and repairs cost $5.

Warranty expense = $10,000 × 2% × $5 = $1,000

Analyzing warranty disclosures

  • GAAP requires that warranty liabilities reflect the estimated cost the company expects to incur as a result of warranty claims.
  • Companies might intentionally distort this estimate:
  • Underestimate the warranty liability to report higher current income
  • Overestimate the warranty liability to depress current income and create a liability (a "cookie jar reserve") to absorb future warranty costs
  • These actions affect income in both the current and subsequent periods — both periods are incorrect.
  • We must closely examine warranty liabilities and scrutinize deviations from the historical relation to sales levels or from peer company levels.

LO 7-2 Short-Term Debt

  • When a company borrows short-term funds, it reports the cash received on the balance sheet together with an increase in liabilities (notes payable).
  • The note is reported as a current liability because the company expects to repay it within a year.
  • The borrower incurs (and the lender earns) interest on the note as time passes.
  • GAAP requires the borrower to accrue the interest liability and the related interest expense each time financial statements are issued.

Worked example. Verizon borrows $1,000 cash on January 1. The note bears 12% interest, payable quarterly.

LO 7-3 Long-Term Debt Pricing

Why bonds

  • When companies require a large amount of financing, issuing bonds in capital markets is a cost-efficient way to raise funds.
  • Bonds are structured like any other borrowing: the borrower receives cash and agrees to pay it back with interest.
  • Generally the entire face amount (principal) of the bond is repaid at maturity, with interest payments made in the interim (usually semiannually).

Issuance. Companies normally work with an underwriter (like Goldman Sachs) to set the terms of the bond issue. The underwriter sells individual bonds (usually in $1,000 denominations) to retail clients and professional portfolio managers (like The Vanguard Group), and receives a fee for underwriting the issue. These bonds are investments for individual investors, other companies, retirement plans, and insurance companies.

Interest rates and bond prices. Issued bonds trade in the secondary market just like stocks. Bond prices fluctuate even though the company's obligation to repay principal and interest remains fixed throughout the life of the bond. The bond's fixed rate of interest can be higher or lower than rates offered on other securities of similar risk, and because bonds compete with other investments, prices are set relative to those alternatives — the laws of supply and demand cause bond prices to rise and fall.

Two interest rates

RateAlso calledWhat it does
Coupon rateContract rate, stated rateStated in the bond contract; used to compute the dollar amount of interest payments paid in cash to bondholders during the life of the issue
Market rateYield, effective rateThe rate of return investors expect to earn; used to price the bond

Cash flows to bondholders. Bondholders expect two types of cash flow: periodic interest payments (usually semiannual) during the bond's life — an annuity, because the payments are equal in amount and made at regular intervals — and a single payment of the face amount at maturity, called a lump-sum because it occurs only once.

Bond price = PV of the annuity payments + PV of the lump-sum payment

Effective cost of debt

  • Bonds are priced to yield the return (market rate) demanded by investors.
  • Thus the effective rate of a bond always equals the yield demanded by investors, regardless of the bond's coupon rate.
  • This means companies cannot influence the effective cost of debt by raising or lowering the coupon rate — doing so will only result in a bond premium or discount.

Interest expense versus interest payments

The effective cost of debt determines the interest expense reported in the issuer's income statement. Because of bond discounts and premiums, interest expense is usually different from the cash interest paid.

Income statement reporting. Interest expense reported on the income statement represents the effective cost of debt, including the cash interest paid (at the coupon rate) plus a portion of the additional borrowing costs associated with the discount (or less a portion of the benefit associated with the premium). The process of recognizing this additional interest expense on a non-par bond is called amortization.

Bond repurchases

Also called bond redemption or bond extinguishment. Companies can, and sometimes do, repurchase their bonds prior to maturity.

From Verizon's note: "Early Debt Redemption Costs — During 2022, we recorded pre-tax early debt redemption costs of $1.2 billion primarily in connection with tender offers. During 2021, we recorded pre-tax early debt redemption costs of $3.5 billion primarily in connection with tender offers, the redemptions of securities issued by Verizon and open market repurchases of various Company and subsidiary notes."

Gain or Loss on Bond Repurchase = Net Bonds Payable − Repurchase Payment
  • The net bonds payable, also referred to as the book value or carrying value, is the net amount reported on the balance sheet.
  • If the issuer pays more to retire the bonds than the amount carried on its balance sheet, it reports a loss on its income statement.
  • The issuer reports a gain on bond retirement if the repurchase price is less than the net bonds payable.

Fair value disclosures

  • GAAP requires companies to report current fair values of their debt in the notes — but not on the balance sheet.
  • Changes in fair values are not included in net income, because gains and losses reverse with subsequent fluctuations in interest rates, and because the bonds are repaid at par at maturity.

LO 7-5 Credit Analysis and the Quality of Debt

The fundamental questions

  • Will the company be able to pay back the amount borrowed?
  • What is the downside risk if the company fails to make payments?

Creditors focus on capital structure (solvency), coverage, and liquidity. They also forecast the company's free operating cash flow and compare it with the expected maturities of the company's debt; the time horizon of that forecast differs depending on the type of credit.

Credit ratings

A credit rating is an opinion of an entity's creditworthiness, captured in alpha-numeric scales. Each rating agency uses its own rating system, and many investment managers are precluded from purchasing noninvestment grade bonds.

The two-step approach. Each agency develops its own proprietary models, but in general the rating agencies take a two-step approach: (1) assess the likelihood of default (the nonpayment of amounts owed), and (2) assess the potential loss the lender will suffer in the event of default. Factors bearing on collectibility in default include:

  • How does the debt rank relative to other issuances by the same borrower?
  • What collateral, if any, has been pledged to secure the debt in the event of nonpayment?
  • What controls and restrictions have the lenders placed on the company to limit risk exposure?

Economics of credit ratings. Lenders require a higher interest rate as the creditworthiness of the borrower declines — this is the risk premium.

Yield Rate = Risk-Free Rate + Risk Premium

Over 2013–2023, BAA-rated corporate yields consistently ran above AAA yields, and both ran above the 10-Year Treasury — the visible price of credit risk.

S&P's general approach. S&P's Corporate Criteria Framework combines a business risk profile (country risk and industry risk, together the CICRA, plus competitive position) with a financial risk profile (cash flow/leverage) to produce an anchor. Modifiers — diversification/portfolio effect, capital structure, financial policy, liquidity, management/governance, and comparable ratings analysis — adjust the anchor to a stand-alone credit profile, which group or government influence then adjusts to the final issuer credit rating.

Capital structure (solvency) analysis

Capital structure is the specific mix of debt and equity used to finance a company's assets and operations. Review the balance sheet to determine debt owed; DuPont analysis uses Total assets ÷ Stockholders' equity. Two other common ratios:

Liabilities-to-equity ratio = Total liabilities ÷ Stockholders' equity
Total debt-to-equity = (Long-term debt and leases including current portion + Short-term debt and leases) ÷ Stockholders' equity

The liabilities-to-equity ratio shows how reliant a company is on creditor financing compared with equity financing. The total debt-to-equity ratio distinguishes between operating creditors and debt obligations.

Coverage analysis

Coverage considers the likelihood that the company will be able to make its required principal and interest payments. Because debt must be repaid with cash, the natural focus is the ability to earn a profit and generate cash from operating activities. Two ratios capture this:

Times interest earned = Earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) ÷ Interest expense, gross
  • Uses interest expense BEFORE interest income is netted
  • Reflects the operating income available to pay interest expense
  • Assumes only interest must be paid and that the principal will be refinanced
Verizon20222021
Times interest earned$30,467 ÷ $3,613 = 8.43$32,448 ÷ $3,485 = 9.31

Verizon can cover its interest expense 8.43 times over.

Cash from operations to total debt = Cash from operations ÷ (Short-term debt + Long-term debt)

Verizon, 2022: $37,141 ÷ $176,331 = 0.21. This measures the ability to generate additional cash to cover debt payments as they come due.

Liquidity analysis

Liquidity refers to cash availability: how much cash a company has, and how much it can generate on short notice.

Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities
Quick ratio = (Cash + Marketable securities + Accounts receivable) ÷ Current liabilities

Current assets are those a company expects to convert into cash within a year; current liabilities are those that come due within a year.

Back-up credit lines are another measure of liquidity — the company's ability to raise additional cash quickly by borrowing under existing credit facilities. Typical covenants include a maximum debt-to-equity ratio, a minimum times interest earned or EBITDA coverage ratio, and a minimum cash from operations / free operating cash flows to total debt.

LO 7-6 Time Value of Money

Present value concepts

Would you rather receive a dollar now, or a dollar one year from now? Most people answer a dollar now — intuition tells us that a dollar received now is more valuable than the same amount received in the future, because the dollar received now could be invested, and one year from now we would have the dollar and the interest earned on it.

Risk and interest factors yield these generalizations:

  • The right to receive an amount now (present value) is worth more than the right to receive the same amount later (future value)
  • The longer we must wait to receive an amount, the less attractive it is
  • The greater the interest rate, the greater the amount we will receive in the future
  • Putting the last two together, the difference between the present value of an amount and its future value is Principal × Interest Rate × Time
  • The more risk associated with a cash flow, the higher the interest rate

Present value computation. If we have $90.91 today and can invest it at 10% for 1 year, our investment will grow to $100:

$90.91 × 1.10 × 1 year = $100 (rounded)

So $90.91 is the present value of $100 to be received in 1 year. Equivalently, at a 10% investment rate we can calculate the present value by discounting the future value: Present Value $90.91 ← discounted for 1 year at 10% ← Future Value $100.

The future value of a single sum is the amount a specific investment is worth at a future date if invested at a given rate of compound interest.

module-8-quick-review-optional.title: Module 8 Quick Review (optional)
module-8-quick-review-optional.body:
Optional quick review, about a two-minute read. Not graded. For more detail, see the full Chapter Review page.

Formulas to know
  • Market capitalization = shares outstanding × share price
  • Book value per share = (stockholders’ equity − preferred stock) ÷ common shares
  • Issuance: cash = common stock (par) + additional paid-in capital
  • Treasury stock (contra-equity) is recorded at cost
  • Stock compensation expense = grant-date fair value ÷ vesting years
  • Dividend payout ratio = dividends ÷ net income
  • Basic EPS = net income ÷ weighted-average shares outstanding

1. Stock as a financing source: market value and book value

  • Market capitalization = shares outstanding × share price.
  • Book value per share = (stockholders’ equity − preferred stock) ÷ common shares outstanding.
  • Market-to-book = market value ÷ book value. A high ratio means investors expect value that the balance sheet does not show.

2. Issuing common stock

  • Cash received is split between common stock (par value) and additional paid-in capital (the amount above par).
  • Assets and equity both increase by the cash received. Net income does not change.
  • More shares outstanding means each share has a claim on a smaller piece of earnings.

3. Repurchasing stock (treasury stock)

  • Treasury stock is a contra-equity account recorded at cost. Cash and total equity both fall by the cost.
  • Treasury shares have no vote and receive no dividends, and they are not counted in EPS.
  • There is no gain or loss on a repurchase. If the shares are resold for more, the difference goes to additional paid-in capital.

4. Stock-based compensation

  • Estimate the fair value of the award at the grant date and record it as expense evenly over the vesting period.
  • The expense reduces net income; the credit increases additional paid-in capital. It is added back on the cash flow statement because it is non-cash.
  • A real cash cost appears when the company buys treasury shares to offset the dilution.

5. Cash dividends

  • Dividends = dividend per share × shares outstanding.
  • A cash dividend reduces cash and retained earnings. It bypasses the income statement.
  • Payout ratio = dividends ÷ net income. Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ share price.

6. Stock splits

  • A split gives shareholders more shares for each share held. It is not a monetary transaction.
  • The number of shares goes up and par value per share goes down by the same factor. Cash, total equity and net income do not change.
  • Prior-period shares and EPS are restated so years remain comparable.

7. Accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI)

  • AOCI is a component of stockholders’ equity. Its changes (other comprehensive income) do not flow through the income statement.
  • Main components: foreign currency translation, employee benefit plans, certain securities, and derivatives and hedges.
  • Comprehensive income = net income + other comprehensive income.

8. Weighted-average shares and basic EPS

  • Weighted-average shares = beginning shares, plus new shares times the fraction of the year outstanding, minus repurchased shares times the fraction of the year they were out.
  • Basic EPS = net income ÷ weighted-average shares outstanding.
  • Weighting matters: the same shares sold in January and in November have very different effects.

9. Why EPS fell more than net income

  • EPS depends on both net income and the share count. If shares rise, EPS falls faster than net income.
  • If shares fall (a repurchase), EPS can rise even when net income is flat.
  • Analysts watch how much of EPS growth comes from earnings and how much from a shrinking share count.

Optional review. Not graded. The running example is Johnson & Johnson (fiscal 2022, $ millions), as in the lectures and textbook.

What this module covers

LOLearning objective
8-1Examine stock as a financing source and explain its various features.
8-2Analyze stock issuances and repurchases.
8-3Interpret stock-based compensation, including restricted stock and options.
8-4Analyze cash dividends and stock splits.
8-5Interpret accumulated other comprehensive income and its components.
8-6Interpret earnings per share.

Running example: Johnson & Johnson, fiscal 2022 (all dollar amounts in millions unless noted), with supporting examples from Danaher (convertible preferred stock), Coca-Cola (stock disclosures), Microsoft (share retirement), Alphabet (stock split), and Eli Lilly and AbbVie (EPS comparison).

The Big Picture: Two Halves of Stockholders’ Equity

Contributed capital — what owners put inEarned capital — what the business generated
AccountsPreferred stock, common stock (at par), additional paid-in capital, less treasury stock (LOs 8-1, 8-2, 8-3)Retained earnings, accumulated other comprehensive income (LOs 8-4, 8-5)
What increases itIssuing shares, resale of treasury shares, stock-based compensationNet income, other comprehensive income
What decreases itRepurchasing shares (treasury stock or retirement)Dividends, comprehensive losses, the excess paid on retired shares

Three threads run through the module. First, transactions with owners never touch the income statement — issuing stock, buying it back, and paying dividends all bypass net income and settle directly in equity. Second, par value is an accounting artifact, not a measure of value; it only splits the issue proceeds between the common stock account and additional paid-in capital. Third, the share count is management’s choice, which is why EPS (LO 8-6) and book value per share tell us much less across companies than they do within one company over time.

LO 8-1 Stock as a Financing Source

Analyzing stockholders’ equity

  • Companies raise funds by selling shares of stock to investors. Unlike creditors, shareholders have no contractual return.
  • The stockholders’ equity section of the balance sheet reports the book value of the stockholders’ investment, as determined under GAAP.
  • Market value is determined by supply and demand in the marketplace as shares are actively traded among investors — it is not what the balance sheet reports.
  • There are two types of stockholders’ equity accounts: contributed capital and earned capital.

LO 8-3 Stock-Based Compensation

Why companies use it

  • Create incentives for employees to act like shareholders. The amount of the award is often tied to corporate performance targets including sales, income, and stock price, motivating employees to make decisions that improve company performance.
  • Encourage employee retention and longevity. Employees earn the right to own or purchase shares over time; this waiting period is the vesting period, during which employees have greater incentive to stay.

Types of plans

PlanHow it works
Restricted stockShares are issued to the employee but the employee is not free to sell them during a restriction period. During that period the employee has the rights of a shareholder other than the ability to sell
Restricted stock units (RSUs)The employee is awarded the right to receive a specified number of shares (or cash equivalent) after a vesting period. Unlike restricted stock, shares are not issued until after the restriction period, at which time the employee has all the rights of a shareholder
Employee stock optionsEmployees are given the right to purchase shares at a fixed (strike) price for a specified period. As with restricted stock, there is a vesting period before the employee can purchase
Stock appreciation rights (SARs)Employees are paid in cash or stock for the increase in share price, but do not purchase shares. Similar to an option, with no share purchase required
Employee share purchase plansEmployees may purchase shares directly from the company at a discount, typically a set percentage (such as 85%) of the prevailing market price

Companies often maintain more than one of these plans at the same time. Most plans contain forfeiture provisions — if the employee is terminated for cause or leaves before vesting, the award is forfeited.

Two analysis issues

IssueWhat it means
1. Expense recognitionWhen shares or options are awarded, companies estimate the fair value of the award and recognize that fair value as compensation expense in the period in which the employee provides service
2. Potential dilutionDilution relates to the number of common shares outstanding that have a claim against the company’s earnings or net assets. Mindful of dilution, companies often repurchase shares in advance to use for stock-based compensation plans

J&J’s note: “The Company settles employee benefit equity issuances with treasury shares. Treasury shares are replenished throughout the year for the number of shares used to settle employee benefit equity issuances.”

Accounting steps

Regardless of the type of plan, the accounting follows common steps:

  • When the award is granted, the company estimates the fair value of the award
  • The fair value is recorded as an expense in the income statement, ratably over the vesting period
  • When the shares are issued, common stock and APIC increase in the same manner as for cash-based stock issuances

Reporting and the cash flow statement

Stock-based compensation expense is included on the income statement but rarely reported as a separate line item. We can, however, determine the amount from the statement of cash flows:

Is stock-based compensation a cash expense?

The add-back might lead some to conclude that this form of compensation is cash free. It is not. A real cash cost occurs when the company buys new treasury shares in the open market to offset the dilution created by the share award. To accurately evaluate and forecast operating cash flow, analysts either:

  • Include stock-based compensation expense — adding it back to calculate non-GAAP measures is not correct, or
  • Recognize the related treasury-stock purchase as an operating cash outflow

LO 8-4 Cash Dividends and Stock Splits

Two topics relate to the earned capital accounts: dividends, which can be paid in cash, other assets, or additional shares of stock (stock dividends); and stock splits, where additional shares are distributed to existing shareholders.

In fiscal 2022, J&J reported dividends per share of $4.45, totaling $11,682 million, and noted that it “increased its dividend in 2022 for the 60th consecutive year.”

Cash dividends — financial effects

Cash dividends reduce cash and retained earnings by the same amount.

Worked example. J&J declares and pays cash dividends of $10 million.

Dividend payments do not affect net income. They directly reduce retained earnings and bypass the income statement.

Stock splits

  • A stock split happens when a company issues additional common shares to its existing stockholders.
  • Splits are usually prompted by the company’s desire to reduce its stock price to improve marketability of the shares.
  • A stock split is not a monetary transaction and, as such, there are no financial statement effects.
  • Companies must disclose the number of shares outstanding for all periods presented, must reduce the par value proportionally, and must adjust historical financial statements presented in the current 10-K likewise.

Stock dividends

One common way to perform a stock split is to declare a dividend payable in company stock.

  • To account for a stock dividend, the company reduces retained earnings (just as for cash dividends) and increases contributed capital accounts.
  • Cash and the stock’s par value per share are both unaffected by a stock dividend.

LO 8-6 Earnings per Share

Basic and diluted EPS

A common metric reported in the financial press is earnings per share (EPS). Companies report two EPS statistics:

Basic EPS = (Net income − Preferred dividends) ÷ Weighted average common shares
Diluted EPS = Basic EPS − EPS impact of dilutive options and warrants − EPS impact of dilutive convertible securities

EPS disclosures are followed obsessively by Wall Street analysts and investors.

Comparing EPS across companies

We cannot compare the EPS of different companies:

  • The number of shares outstanding is not proportional to income
  • Management controls the number of common shares outstanding
  • There is no relation between firm size and EPS
